segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the other side of the sea, to the region of the Gerasenes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he got out of the boat, immediately a man with an unclean spirit came out of the tombs to meet him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He lived among the tombs, and no one could bind him any longer, not even with a chain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he had torn the chains apart and smashed the shackles, and no one was strong enough to subdue him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Constantly, night and day, among the tombs and in the hills, he was crying out and cutting himself with stones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and crying out in a loud voice he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you have to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I charge you by God, do not torment me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he had been saying to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he asked him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is your name?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My name is Legion, for we are many.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now a large herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they begged him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send us into the pigs, so that we may enter them.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs, and the herd, about two thousand of them, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and were drowned in the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had been tending them fled and reported it in the town and in the countryside, and people came to see what it was that had happened.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind—the very man who had had the legion—and they were afraid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man, and told them about the pigs.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they began to beg him to leave their territory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been demon-possessed begged him that he might be with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not let him, but said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go home to your own people and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he had mercy on you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone was amazed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was beside the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came, and when he saw him he fell at his feet

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and begged him earnestly,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he went with him. A large crowd was following him and pressing in on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had endured much under many doctors and had spent everything she had, yet she had gained nothing by it but had instead grown worse.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had heard about Jesus, and she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for she was saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If I touch even his clothes, I will be made well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately the source of her bleeding dried up, and she knew in her body that she was healed of her affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And immediately Jesus, aware in himself that power had gone out from him, turned around in the crowd and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who touched my clothes?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You see the crowd pressing in on you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he kept looking around to see the woman who had done this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the woman, afraid and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be cured of your affliction.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any further?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, ignoring what was said, told the synagogue leader,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid; only believe.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not let anyone accompany him except Peter, James, and John the brother of James.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to the synagogue leader’s house, and he saw a commotion, with people weeping and wailing loudly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went in and said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child has not died but is sleeping.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they laughed at him. But he put them all out, took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him, and went in where the child was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking the child by the hand, he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Talitha koum,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which translated means,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Little girl, I say to you, get up!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Immediately the girl got up and began walking around, for she was twelve years old. And immediately they were overcome with great astonishment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He gave them strict orders that no one should know about this, and told them to give her something to eat.

notes.note: Manuscripts differ here between “Gerasenes,” “Gadarenes,” and “Gergesenes.” Gerasa lay roughly thirty miles southeast of the lake, which is probably why copyists substituted the names of nearer places. Most editors judge “Gerasenes” to be the original reading in Mark.

The Greek verb names the act of prostrating oneself, and what it signifies depends on who does it and to whom. Here a possessed man throws himself down before a superior power he fears, so the gesture is rendered instead of “worship,” which in modern English implies devotion. Most recent versions likewise have “bowed down” or “fell on his knees” here.

The verb means to put someone under a solemn oath, and it was the kind of formula exorcists used to command spirits (compare Acts 19:13). Here the roles are reversed: the spirit tries the exorcist’s formula on Jesus, and it has no effect.

A Latin military term for the main unit of the Roman army, some five to six thousand soldiers at full strength. As the speaker explains, it stands here for a very large number. Whether Mark also intends an allusion to the Roman occupation is debated.

Spoken by Jesus, “the Lord” most naturally refers to God, and Luke’s parallel has “God.” The next verse, however, has the man proclaim what “Jesus” had done for him, and Mark may intend the reader to notice the overlap.

A group of ten Hellenistic cities, most of them east of the Jordan, with largely non-Jewish populations. The herd of pigs, animals unclean under the Law, has already signaled that the scene is set in Gentile territory.

The phrase echoes the Greek of Leviticus 15, where chronic bleeding of this kind makes a woman ritually unclean, along with whatever she touches. Mark does not mention impurity, and scholars disagree about how far it shapes the scene. It may help explain her secrecy and her fear.

The verb here and in verses 23 and 28 is the one usually translated “save.” In Greek it covers rescue from any danger, including illness, and in this story physical healing is the primary sense. Many interpreters think Mark also means the reader to hear the wider sense, “your faith has saved you.”

The Greek verb can mean either “overhear” or “pay no attention to, disregard.” The second is its regular sense in the Septuagint and at Matthew 18:17, and is followed here, but many translations have “overhearing” and either fits the scene. Many later manuscripts read simply “hearing,” which is the reading behind the King James Version.

These words are Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus and of Galilee, which Mark preserves and then translates for his Greek-speaking readers. Many manuscripts read “koumi,” the grammatically feminine form of the imperative. The phrase “I say to you” in Mark’s translation is not represented in the Aramaic words themselves.

candidates.reason: The same verb means both heal and save, and translators split between “made you well” and “saved you” in healing stories across the Gospels, so the formula “your faith has σέσωκέν you” needs one policy.
Recurs across the Gospels and is rendered variously as “demon-possessed,” “demonized,” or “possessed by demons,” and the choice affects how readers picture the condition.
Mark’s signature adverb occurs some forty times, and versions vary between “immediately,” “at once,” “just then,” and omission, obscuring a deliberate stylistic feature.
This title recurs in Mark, Luke and Acts and is rendered “ruler of the synagogue,” “synagogue leader,” or “synagogue official,” so it needs one fixed English form.
Very frequent across the New Testament with senses ranging from beg and urge to encourage and comfort, so the sense boundaries and the English for each need fixing.
